props.title: Crime and Punishment

sections.content: Josef von Sternberg's adaptation of Crime and Punishment (1935) marked one of Hollywood's first serious attempts to tackle Dostoyevsky's psychological masterpiece. Peter Lorre delivers a haunting performance as Raskolnikov, bringing his signature nervous energy from M (1931) to create a tortured anti-hero consumed by moral philosophy and murder. The film streamlines the novel's complex narrative while maintaining its core exploration of guilt, redemption, and psychological torment. While some critics dismissed it as oversimplified, the film's expressionistic lighting and claustrophobic framing effectively translate Raskolnikov's deteriorating mental state to the screen. Crime and Punishment|1935|Peter Lorre stars in von Sternberg's adaptation of Dostoyevsky's novel about a student who commits murder to prove his superiority|Criterion M|1931|Fritz Lang's masterpiece about a child murderer hunted by both police and criminals, starring Peter Lorre|HBO Max Notes from Underground|1995|Adaptation of another Dostoyevsky work exploring alienation and moral philosophy|Prime

The 1930s saw several bold attempts to bring Russian literature to Hollywood screens. Anna Karenina (1935) with Greta Garbo demonstrated how star power could make challenging material accessible, while The Brothers Karamazov (1937) proved that even Dostoyevsky's most philosophically dense work could be adapted. These films established a template for literary adaptations that influenced later works like Crime and Punishment with George Hamilton and the BBC's Crime and Punishment.

Von Sternberg's version stands out for its visual style, importing German Expressionist techniques to create a psychological thriller. The director's experience with films like The Blue Angel (1930) helped him craft scenes where shadow and light externalize Raskolnikov's internal struggle. This approach influenced later film noir classics like Double Indemnity (1944) and The Third Man (1949), which similarly used expressionist techniques to explore guilt and moral corruption. Double Indemnity|1944|Billy Wilder's noir masterpiece about murder and insurance fraud|Criterion The Third Man|1949|Carol Reed's atmospheric thriller set in post-war Vienna|Criterion The Blue Angel|1930|Von Sternberg's classic starring Marlene Dietrich as a cabaret performer|TCM SUBHEAD: Modern Interpretations and Influence

Contemporary filmmakers continue drawing inspiration from Dostoyevsky's themes of guilt and redemption. Match Point (2005) transposes elements of Crime and Punishment to modern London, while American Psycho (2000) offers a satirical take on Raskolnikov's superiority complex. Woody Allen's Crimes and Misdemeanors (1989) directly engages with Dostoyevsky's moral questions about murder and conscience in a modern context.
